title: Chapter 49 — The Hyena
paragraphs: There are certain queer times and occasions in this strange mixed affair we call life when a man takes the whole universe for a vast practical joke, though the humor of it he can only dimly see, and more than suspects that the joke is at nobody's expense but his own. However, nothing discourages him, and nothing seems worth arguing about. He swallows down all events, all creeds, all beliefs, all hard things visible and invisible, no matter how lumpy — as an ostrich with a powerful digestion gobbles down bullets and gun flints. And just as the ostrich blindly swallows these things, so does this man greedily consume the strangest opinions.

"Queequeg," I said, when they had dragged me — the last man — to the deck, and I was still shaking myself in my jacket to fling off the water, "Queequeg, my fine friend, does this sort of thing happen often?" Without much emotion, though soaked through just like me, he gave me to understand that such things did often happen.

"Mr. Stubb," I said, turning to that worthy, who, buttoned up in his oil jacket, was now calmly smoking his pipe in the rain, "Mr. Stubb, I think I have heard you say that of all whalemen you ever met, our chief mate, Mr. Starbuck, is by far the most careful and prudent. I suppose, then, that going headlong at a running whale with your sail set in a foggy squall is the height of a whaleman's discretion?"
"Certainly. I've lowered for whales from a leaking ship in a gale off Cape Horn."

"Mr. Flask," I said, turning to little King-Post, who was standing close by, "you are experienced in these things, and I am not. Will you tell me whether it is an unbreakable law in this fishery, Mr. Flask, for an oarsman to break his own back pulling himself backward into death's jaws?"

"Can't you put it more simply?" said Flask. "Yes, that's the law. I'd like to see a boat's crew backing water up to a whale face-first. Ha, ha! The whale would give them squint for squint, mind that!"

Here, then, from three impartial witnesses, I had a deliberate statement of the entire situation. Considering, therefore, that squalls and capsizings and consequent campouts on the deep were matters of common occurrence in this kind of life — considering that at the supremely critical moment of approaching the whale, I must trust my life to the man who steered the boat, often a fellow who at that very instant was so reckless as to nearly sink the craft with his own excitement — considering that the particular danger of my situation was that I always belonged to the harpooner's boat, and the harpooner's duty was to approach nearest to the whale's head — and considering finally that in these critical moments the harpooner's task was to stand up and throw his weapon from a frantically rocking boat — considering all this, I say, it seemed to me that making a rough draft of my last will and testament was the sensible thing to do.

It may seem strange that of all men, sailors should be so fond of tinkering at their last wills and testaments, but there are no people in the world more devoted to that pastime. This was the fourth time in my nautical career that I had done the same thing. After the ceremony was concluded, I felt much easier. A stone was rolled away from my heart. Besides, all the days I should now live would be as good as the days that Lazarus lived after his resurrection — a supplementary clean gain of so many months or weeks as the case might be. I survived myself. My death and burial were locked up in my chest. I looked around me, calm and collected, and made up my mind to be coolly brave from that moment forward.
Now then, I thought, unconsciously rolling up my sleeves — here goes for a cool, collected dive at death and destruction, and the devil take the hindmost.
